chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from one of his companions, from Aban ibn Uthman, from the one who informed him, from one of the two Imams (peace be upon them) who said:

A man was brought to Umar ibn al-Khattab who had killed a brother of a man, so he handed him over to him and ordered him to kill him. The man struck him until he saw that he had killed him, so he was carried to his house, and they found him to have a remnant of life (barely alive), so they treated him and he was cured.

So when he went out, the brother of the first killed man seized him and said, 'You are the killer of my brother, and it is for me to kill you.' He said, 'You have already killed me once.' So he took him to Umar, who ordered him to be killed. He went out saying, 'By Allah, you have already killed me once.'

So they passed by Amir al-Mu'minin (peace be upon him) and informed him of his news. He said, 'Do not be hasty until I come out to you.' So he entered upon Umar and said, 'The judgement regarding him is not like this.' Umar said, 'And what is it, O Abu al-Hasan?'

He said, 'This man (the brother of the deceased) has the right to do to the brother of the first killed man what he did to him, then he can kill him in retaliation for his brother.' The man realized that if he retaliated, it would come upon his own soul, so he forgave him, and they both left.

key_terms.أَخِي الْمَقْتُولِ الْأَوَّلِ: The brother of the first killed man
key_terms.رَمَقاً: A remnant of life; barely alive

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on retaliation when a killer survives being killed by the victim's brother?
ai.summary: This hadith illustrates the jurisprudential distinction between *qisas* (retaliation) and *daman* (blood money) in Shia jurisprudence, where Imam Ali (AS) clarifies that the heir of the first victim holds the exclusive right to choose between execution or compensation for the initial killing. The narrative highlights the practical application of *ta'abbun* (taking back) in cases of double homicide, demonstrating how the victim's heir can strategically forgive the killer to preserve his own life, thereby avoiding a second retaliatory strike. This case is frequently cited by scholars to discuss the nuances of *qisas* when multiple victims are involved in a single perpetrator's actions.
